chapter.title: Chapter 6: Full Workbook and Self-Assessment
chapter.description: A full exam-condition workbook combining twenty sentence transformations, five complete Band 6.0 Task 2 essays for rewriting to Band 8.5–9.0, and five complete IELTS Speaking Part 2 and Part 3 simulations with model responses.
learning_objectives: Transform flat Band 6.0 sentences into precise Band 9.0 sentences.

Practise IELTS Speaking Part 2 long turns under one-minute planning and two-minute speaking conditions.
Develop natural spoken-register idioms and collocations for Speaking Part 2 and Part 3.
Move from conversational narrative in Speaking Part 2 toward more analytical language in Part 3.

blocks.title: Full Workbook and Self-Assessment
blocks.content: This chapter is where everything in the book comes together under exam conditions. Part 1 contains two workouts: twenty sentence transformations that take a flat Band 6 sentence up to a polished Band 9 one, and five complete Band 6 essays for you to rewrite at Band 8.5 to 9.0. Part 2 contains five full Speaking simulations with model responses. Work with a pen, attempt every item before reading the model, and mark your own version against the key by asking which specific tool from Chapters 1 to 5 you failed to apply.

blocks.title: Section 1: 20 Sentence Transformation Challenges
blocks.instructions: Each sentence below is written at roughly Band 6.0. Rewrite each one as a single Band 9.0 sentence, upgrading the vocabulary, fixing any first-language errors, and tightening the structure. Aim for precision, not just longer words. Model answers are in the key at the end of this file.

questions.prompt: Nowadays, technology is a very important thing in our life.
Many people think that money can make them happy.

The government should give more money to education.

Cutting trees is a very bad thing for the environment.

blocks.title: Section 2: Five Full Essay Rewrites
blocks.instructions: Below are five complete Band 6.0 essays, one for each of the main Task 2 question types. Each contains the exact weaknesses this book targets: overused words, weak linkers, and first-language slips. Your task is to rewrite each essay at Band 8.5 to 9.0, keeping the ideas but upgrading the language throughout. Full model rewrites are in the key.

essays.prompt: Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essays.draft:
Nowadays, education is a very important thing for everyone. Some people think that university education should be free for all students. I am agree with this idea because it has many good points.

First, free university can help poor students. Many talented students cannot go to university because it is very costly. If education is free, they can also get a chance to study and get a good job. This is good for the whole country because it makes more skilled people.

But some people say that free education is a big problem for the government. The government has to spend a lot of money and this money comes from tax. Also, if university is free, maybe some students will not study seriously.

However, I think the advantages are more than the disadvantages. A country becomes strong when its people are educated. So the government should give importance on free education.

In conclusion, I agree that university education should be free because it helps poor students and it is good for the country.
essays.model_answer:
It is often argued that university education should be provided free of charge to all students. I strongly agree with this view, primarily because it widens access and strengthens the economy in the long run.

The most compelling argument concerns equality of opportunity. At present, many talented young people are unable to attend university because tuition fees are prohibitively expensive. If higher education were free, these students could also pursue their ambitions and secure well-paid employment. Society as a whole would reap the benefits, since a larger pool of skilled graduates drives national productivity.

Admittedly, critics contend that free education places a heavy financial burden on the state, funded ultimately through taxation. They further argue that students may value their studies less when they cost nothing.

Nevertheless, these drawbacks are outweighed by the wider gains. A nation prospers when its population is well educated, and public investment in universities tends to pay for itself through higher earnings and tax revenue. Governments should therefore prioritise funding for higher education.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that university education should be free, as it removes financial barriers for disadvantaged students and yields lasting benefits for the country.
essays.key_upgrades: I am agree to I strongly agree; give importance on to prioritise; but to Admittedly and Nevertheless; a second conditional (if … were free … could); collocations reap the benefits, place a burden on, drive productivity.

essays.prompt: Some people think children should start school at a very early age. Others believe they should start later. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essays.draft:
There is a big debate about when children should start school. Some people think children should start school when they are very young. Other people think it is better to start later. In this essay I will discuss about both sides.

On one hand, starting school early has many good points. Young children can learn many things quickly. They also learn how to make friends and follow rules. This helps them in the future.

On the other hand, some people think early school is bad for children. Small children need to play and they should not have pressure. If they start too early, maybe they will not enjoy their childhood. Also, they can feel stress.

In my opinion, both sides have good points. But I think it is better to start school at a normal age, not too early and not too late. Children should learn but they should also have time to play.

In conclusion, there are different opinions about this topic. I think a balance is the best way for children.
essays.model_answer:
There is considerable debate about the ideal age for children to begin formal schooling. While some argue that children should start as early as possible, others maintain that a later start is preferable. This essay will examine both views before giving my opinion.

On the one hand, an early start offers clear advantages. Young children absorb new knowledge remarkably quickly, and school helps them develop social skills such as making friends and following rules, which benefit them throughout life.

On the other hand, critics contend that beginning school too soon can be detrimental. Young children need ample time to play and should not face academic pressure prematurely; otherwise, they may lose the freedom of childhood and experience unnecessary stress.

From my perspective, both positions have merit, but the most sensible approach is to strike a balance: children should begin at a moderate age, neither too early nor too late, so that structured learning and free play can coexist.

In conclusion, although opinions on this issue differ, I believe a balanced starting age best serves children’s long-term development.
essays.key_upgrades: discuss about to examine; good points to advantages and merit; bad to detrimental; strike a balance; on the one hand … on the other hand used precisely.

essays.prompt: Traffic congestion is a growing problem in many cities. What are the causes, and what solutions can you suggest?
essays.draft:
Traffic congestion is a very big problem in many cities today. There are many causes of this problem and we can find some solutions also.

The main cause is that there are too many cars on the road. Nowadays, many people can buy their own car, so the roads become full. Another cause is that public transport is not good in many cities, so people prefer private cars. Also, roads are old and small.

This problem causes many difficulties. People waste a lot of time in traffic and it also creates pollution.

There are some solutions for this problem. First, the government should make public transport better so that people use it. Second, they can build more roads and flyovers. Also, they can make a rule to reduce cars in the city center.

In conclusion, traffic congestion is a serious problem but it can be solved if the government takes good steps.
essays.model_answer:
Traffic congestion has become a pressing problem in many cities. This essay will outline its principal causes before proposing several viable solutions.

The primary cause is the sheer number of vehicles on the roads. As incomes rise, private car ownership has soared, leaving streets heavily congested. A further factor is inadequate public transport, which pushes commuters toward private cars, while ageing and narrow road networks compound the problem. The consequences are significant: commuters waste countless hours in gridlock, and vehicle emissions worsen urban air quality.

Fortunately, the issue can be addressed. Governments should first invest in efficient mass transit so that commuters have an attractive alternative to driving. Expanding the road network and building flyovers would ease the burden on existing routes. In addition, introducing a congestion charge would discourage private car use in city centres.

In conclusion, although traffic congestion is a serious problem, it can be substantially reduced if authorities implement effective measures, particularly by improving public transport and discouraging unnecessary car journeys.
essays.key_upgrades: very big problem to pressing problem; soared, gridlock, ease the burden, congestion charge, implement effective measures; also to A further factor and In addition.

essays.prompt: More and more people are working from home. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
essays.draft:
These days, more and more people are working from home. Some people think it has many advantages, but others think it has disadvantages. In my opinion, the advantages are more.

There are many good things about working from home. First, people can save time because they do not need to travel to office. So they can spend this time with family. Second, they feel relaxed and comfortable in their home.

But there are also some bad things. When people work from home, they can feel lonely. Also, sometimes it is difficult to focus because of family and other distractions. Some people also work less.

However, I think the advantages are bigger. With good discipline, people can do their work properly at home. Companies also save money on office rent.

In conclusion, working from home has both good and bad sides, but I believe the advantages are more than the disadvantages.
essays.model_answer:
In recent years, remote working has become increasingly widespread. While it carries certain drawbacks, I firmly believe that its advantages outweigh them.

The benefits are considerable. Firstly, employees no longer need to commute, which saves a great deal of time that can instead be spent with family. Secondly, working in the comfort of one’s own home can reduce stress and improve wellbeing.

Admittedly, there are disadvantages. Remote workers may feel isolated from colleagues, and domestic distractions can make it difficult to concentrate; a minority may also become less productive without direct supervision.

Nevertheless, these drawbacks can largely be overcome. With sufficient self-discipline, most people can work just as effectively from home, and employers benefit too, since they can reduce expenditure on office space. On balance, the flexibility and savings that remote working offers are more significant than its shortcomings.

In conclusion, although working from home has both merits and limitations, I am convinced that its advantages, particularly greater flexibility and reduced commuting, clearly outweigh the disadvantages.
essays.key_upgrades: good things and bad things to benefits and drawbacks; bigger to outweigh; reduce expenditure; On balance; the advantages are more to its advantages clearly outweigh.

essays.prompt: Many people today prefer fast food to home-cooked meals. Why is this? Is it a positive or negative development?
essays.draft:
Nowadays, many people prefer fast food instead of home-cooked meals. There are some reasons for this and I think it is a negative development.

There are many reasons why people like fast food. The main reason is that people are very busy today, so they do not have time to cook. Fast food is quick and easy. Another reason is that fast food is tasty and cheap. Also, there are many fast food shops everywhere.

However, I think this is a negative thing. Fast food has a lot of fat and sugar, so it is very bad for health. It causes many diseases like obesity. Home-cooked food is more healthy and clean.

In conclusion, people prefer fast food because it is quick and cheap, but I think it is a negative development because it is bad for our health.
essays.model_answer:
These days, a growing number of people favour fast food over home-cooked meals. This essay will explain why this shift has occurred and argue that it is, on balance, a negative development.

Several factors explain the trend. The primary reason is the hectic pace of modern life: many people simply lack the time to prepare meals, and fast food is quick and convenient. In addition, it is inexpensive and palatable, and outlets are now ubiquitous in most cities.

However, I regard this development as largely detrimental. Fast food is typically high in fat, salt, and sugar, and therefore has a harmful effect on health, contributing to conditions such as obesity and heart disease. Home-cooked meals, by contrast, are generally more nutritious and hygienic.

In conclusion, although people increasingly turn to fast food because it is fast and affordable, I believe the trend is a negative one, since it poses a serious threat to public health.
essays.key_upgrades: prefer … instead of to favour … over; tasty to palatable; everywhere to ubiquitous; very bad for health to has a harmful effect on health and poses a serious threat to public health.

answer_key.note: The source provides worked Band 8.5–9.0 model rewrites and key upgrades for all five essays.

blocks.title: Part 2: Five Speaking Simulations
blocks.content: This second half of the workbook contains five complete Speaking simulations, each with a Part 2 cue card, a model long-turn answer, a set of Part 3 follow-up questions with model answers, and a short lexical analysis. The models are written in natural spoken register, so they use contractions and idioms freely. That is exactly right for Speaking, and exactly wrong for Writing Task 2: notice how the idiomatic language that lifts these answers is the same language Chapter 5 told you to keep out of your essays.
how_to_use: Give yourself one minute to plan.
Speak for two minutes before reading the model.
Underline every idiom and collocation in the model.
Check whether you produced anything at that level.
Use the lexical analysis to identify what the examiner would have rewarded.

blocks.title: Simulation 1

part2.title: Describe a place you enjoy visiting.

blocks.model_long_turn:
I’d like to talk about a small hill town called Bandarban, in the southeast of Bangladesh. It isn’t exactly a stone’s throw away from where I live, so I only manage to go there once in a blue moon, maybe once a year, but it’s always worth the long journey.

What I love about it is that it’s completely off the beaten track. While a lot of tourists head to the crowded beaches, Bandarban is quieter and surrounded by breathtaking scenery: green hills, winding rivers, and tiny villages. When I’m there, I usually go hiking, explore the local markets, and just soak up the peace and quiet.

The main reason I enjoy it so much is that it gives me a real change of scenery. Living in a busy city, I’m always caught up in the daily grind, so escaping to the hills feels like a breath of fresh air. The last time I went, I reached the top of a hill right at sunrise, and honestly, that view was the icing on the cake. It was almost the trip of a lifetime, and I came back feeling completely recharged.

part3.question: Why do people enjoy travelling to new places?
part3.answer: I think travel broadens people’s horizons. When you visit somewhere unfamiliar, you experience a different culture and way of life, which gives you a fresh perspective. For a lot of people it’s also a chance to escape their routine and recharge, so it’s really the best of both worlds: you relax and you learn something at the same time.

part3.question: Does tourism benefit local communities?
part3.answer: By and large, yes. Tourism can boost the local economy and create jobs, especially in remote areas. That said, it’s a bit of a double-edged sword, because mass tourism can put a strain on local resources and even degrade natural attractions, so it has to be managed carefully.

part3.question: Do people travel more now than in the past?
part3.answer: Definitely. Air travel has become far more affordable, and social media makes distant places look appealing, so more people have caught the travel bug. In the past, international travel was a luxury; nowadays, it’s within reach for the average family.

blocks.lexical_analysis: The long turn earns its marks through natural idioms (a stone’s throw away, once in a blue moon, off the beaten track, a change of scenery, the daily grind, a breath of fresh air, the icing on the cake, the trip of a lifetime) woven into fluent description, plus the collocation breathtaking scenery. In Part 3 the register shifts slightly toward discussion, bringing in broaden horizons, the best of both worlds, boost the local economy, a double-edged sword, and put a strain on. Every one of these belongs in Speaking; not one belongs in a Task 2 essay.

blocks.title: Simulation 2

part2.title: Describe a skill you would like to learn.
prompts: why you want to learn it

blocks.model_long_turn:
A skill I’d really love to learn is playing the guitar. I’ve wanted to pick it up for years, but I’ve never had the time to properly sit down and practise.

I’d probably learn it through a mix of online tutorials and a local teacher, because I think I’d need someone to help me get the hang of the basics. I imagine it would be a steep learning curve at first, especially learning the chords, and I’d have to burn the midnight oil to make real progress. Realistically, it might take a year or so before I could play a full song without stumbling.

The main reason I want to learn it is that music is a wonderful way to unwind after a long day. At the moment I’m caught up in the daily grind, and I think playing an instrument would help me relax and switch off completely. On top of that, being able to play at family gatherings would be the icing on the cake. Even if I’m never brilliant at it, I’d be over the moon just to strum a few tunes for the people I love.

part3.question: Is it better to learn a skill from a teacher or by yourself?
part3.answer: It depends on the skill, but I think a teacher gives you a real head start. They can spot your mistakes and stop you from picking up bad habits. That said, teaching yourself builds discipline, so ideally you’d combine the two and get the best of both worlds.

part3.question: Why do some people find it hard to learn new skills as adults?
part3.answer: More often than not, it comes down to time and confidence. Adults are busy and afraid of failing, so they give up before they really get to grips with it. Children, by contrast, learn through trial and error without worrying about looking silly.

part3.question: Should schools teach more practical skills?
part3.answer: Absolutely. I’d argue that schools place too much emphasis on exams and not enough on practical, transferable skills. Teaching things like budgeting or basic coding would equip students far better for real life.

blocks.lexical_analysis: The long turn leans on study and effort idioms (pick it up, get the hang of, a steep learning curve, burn the midnight oil, the daily grind, switch off, the icing on the cake, over the moon) and the natural verb unwind. Part 3 raises the register with a head start, the best of both worlds, get to grips with, trial and error, and the essay-style collocations place emphasis on, transferable skills, and equip students, which show the candidate can move between casual narrative and reasoned argument.

blocks.title: Simulation 3

part2.title: Describe a piece of technology you find useful.
prompts: why it is so useful to you

blocks.model_long_turn:
The piece of technology I find most useful is, without a doubt, my smartphone. It sounds obvious, but I honestly couldn’t get through the day without it. I use it around the clock, from the moment I wake up to the moment I go to sleep.

I rely on it for pretty much everything: checking emails, navigating unfamiliar streets, paying bills, and staying in touch with family. Because so much information is at my fingertips, tasks that used to take hours are now a piece of cake. If I need directions, for instance, I no longer have to ask around; I just tap the screen and go.

The main reason it’s so useful is that it’s basically several devices rolled into one, so it saves me a huge amount of time. Of course, it’s a bit of a double-edged sword, because I can easily end up glued to the screen, but as long as I keep it in check, the benefits far outweigh that. For me, it’s genuinely a game changer, and it’s honestly hard to imagine going back to life without it.

part3.question: Has technology made people’s lives easier or more stressful?
part3.answer: It’s genuinely both. On the one hand, technology has transformed the way we work and communicate, making everything faster. On the other, being constantly connected can be exhausting, and a lot of people struggle to switch off. So I’d say it’s a mixed blessing.

part3.question: Do you think people rely too much on technology?
part3.answer: More often than not, yes. Many of us can’t navigate without a map app or even remember a phone number anymore. It’s convenient, but it does make you wonder whether we’re quietly losing some basic skills along the way.

part3.question: How might technology change the way we work in the future?
part3.answer: I imagine automation will reshape the job market completely. A lot of routine tasks will be automated, which could render some jobs obsolete, but it should also create brand-new roles. The key will be helping people keep up with the times through proper retraining.

blocks.lexical_analysis: The long turn uses tech-flavoured idioms (around the clock, at my fingertips, a piece of cake, a double-edged sword, glued to the screen, keep it in check, a game changer) to sound effortless. Part 3 brings in the formal-leaning collocations transform the way we, a mixed blessing, reshape the job market, render obsolete, and keep up with the times. This is a good illustration of a candidate who can be conversational in Part 2 and more analytical in Part 3 without ever slipping into essay stiffness.

blocks.title: Simulation 4

part2.title: Describe a time when you helped someone.
prompts: how you felt about helping them

blocks.model_long_turn:
I’d like to talk about a time I helped a younger cousin of mine who was struggling with his studies. He was in at the deep end, preparing for a big exam, and he was really down in the dumps because he’d fallen badly behind.

I offered to lend a hand and tutor him a couple of evenings a week. We went through the topics he found difficult, and I tried to help him get to grips with the trickier concepts. It wasn’t always a piece of cake, because he’d lost a lot of confidence, so I had to go the extra mile to keep him motivated.

He needed help because both his parents worked long hours and couldn’t sit with him, so he’d basically been left to cope on his own. In the end, he pulled his socks up and passed with flying colours.

Honestly, I was over the moon when I heard the result. Helping him turned out to be a real labour of love, and seeing him succeed was the icing on the cake. It reminded me just how rewarding it is to give someone a helping hand when they need it.

part3.question: Why is it important to help others in society?
part3.answer: I think helping others creates a stronger sense of community. When people lend a hand, it builds trust and mutual support, which benefits everyone. A society where people only look out for themselves tends to be far more divided.

part3.question: Should helping others be taught in schools?
part3.answer: Definitely. Schools play a pivotal role in shaping a child’s character, so encouraging students to volunteer instils values like empathy and responsibility. If children learn to help early on, it usually stays with them for life.

part3.question: Do people help each other less than they used to?
part3.answer: It’s hard to say, but many would argue that busy, urban lifestyles have made people more self-centred. That said, social media has also made it easier to organise help quickly, so in some ways the spirit of helping is alive and well, just in a different form.

blocks.lexical_analysis: This long turn is dense with natural idioms because it narrates an experience: in at the deep end, down in the dumps, lend a hand, get to grips with, a piece of cake, go the extra mile, pull his socks up, pass with flying colours, over the moon, a labour of love, the icing on the cake, and a helping hand. Used together but not forced, they signal genuine fluency. Part 3 then reaches for the more academic play a pivotal role in, shaping character, and instil values, which fit an abstract discussion of society.

blocks.title: Simulation 5

part2.title: Describe an environmental problem in your area.
prompts: what could be done to solve it

blocks.model_long_turn:
The biggest environmental problem in my city is air pollution, which has become a really pressing concern over the last few years. On a bad day, the air is so hazy that you can barely see across the street.

The main causes are the sheer number of vehicles on the roads and the emissions from nearby factories. Because the city has grown so quickly, the infrastructure simply hasn’t kept up, so traffic is bumper to bumper for most of the day, and all those vehicles emit huge amounts of pollution.

It affects people in a big way. Many residents suffer from breathing problems, and children and the elderly are hit the hardest. Honestly, on some mornings it feels like the whole city grinds to a halt under a blanket of smog.

As for solutions, I think the authorities need to invest in public transport and gradually discourage private car use, perhaps through a congestion charge. Planting more trees and creating green spaces would help too. It certainly won’t be solved overnight, but if everyone plays their part, I’m hopeful things can improve.

part3.question: Whose responsibility is it to protect the environment?
part3.answer: I’d say it’s a shared responsibility. Governments need to implement effective measures and regulate industry, but individuals also have to play their part by cutting their carbon footprint. Neither side can solve it alone.

part3.question: Are people today more environmentally aware than before?
part3.answer: By and large, yes. People are far more conscious of issues like climate change, and going green has become quite mainstream. That said, awareness doesn’t always translate into action, so there’s still a long way to go.

part3.question: Can technology solve environmental problems?
part3.answer: To a certain extent. Renewable energy and cleaner transport are genuine game changers that could mitigate a lot of damage. But technology alone isn’t a silver bullet; it has to go hand in hand with real changes in how we live and consume.

blocks.lexical_analysis: Because this topic is closer to an essay theme, the long turn blends natural idioms (bumper to bumper, grinds to a halt, play their part) with topic collocations that also appear in Chapter 4 (a pressing concern, emissions, infrastructure, invest in public transport, discourage private car use, congestion charge, green spaces). Part 3 pushes further into argument language: implement effective measures, carbon footprint, going green, mitigate, a game changer, a silver bullet, and go hand in hand. This shows the useful overlap between Speaking Part 3 and essay vocabulary, while the idioms keep the delivery sounding spoken rather than recited.

Section 2: Five Full Essay Rewrites
Below are five complete Band 6.0 essays, one for each of the main Task 2 question types. Each contains the exact weaknesses this book targets: overused words, weak linkers, and first-language slips. Your task is to rewrite each essay at Band 8.5 to 9.0, keeping the ideas but upgrading the language throughout. Full model rewrites are in the key.

Essay 1 (Opinion) · Band 6.0 draft
Prompt: Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Draft: Nowadays, education is a very important thing for everyone. Some people think that university education should be free for all students. I am agree with this idea because it has many good points.

First, free university can help poor students. Many talented students cannot go to university because it is very costly. If education is free, they can also get a chance to study and get a good job. This is good for the whole country because it makes more skilled people.

But some people say that free education is a big problem for the government. The government has to spend a lot of money and this money comes from tax. Also, if university is free, maybe some students will not study seriously.

However, I think the advantages are more than the disadvantages. A country becomes strong when its people are educated. So the government should give importance on free education.

In conclusion, I agree that university education should be free because it helps poor students and it is good for the country.

Essay 2 (Discuss both views) · Band 6.0 draft
Prompt: Some people think children should start school at a very early age. Others believe they should start later. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Draft: There is a big debate about when children should start school. Some people think children should start school when they are very young. Other people think it is better to start later. In this essay I will discuss about both sides.

On one hand, starting school early has many good points. Young children can learn many things quickly. They also learn how to make friends and follow rules. This helps them in the future.

On the other hand, some people think early school is bad for children. Small children need to play and they should not have pressure. If they start too early, maybe they will not enjoy their childhood. Also, they can feel stress.

In my opinion, both sides have good points. But I think it is better to start school at a normal age, not too early and not too late. Children should learn but they should also have time to play.

In conclusion, there are different opinions about this topic. I think a balance is the best way for children.

Essay 3 (Problem and solution) · Band 6.0 draft
Prompt: Traffic congestion is a growing problem in many cities. What are the causes, and what solutions can you suggest?
Draft: Traffic congestion is a very big problem in many cities today. There are many causes of this problem and we can find some solutions also.

The main cause is that there are too many cars on the road. Nowadays, many people can buy their own car, so the roads become full. Another cause is that public transport is not good in many cities, so people prefer private cars. Also, roads are old and small.

This problem causes many difficulties. People waste a lot of time in traffic and it also creates pollution.

There are some solutions for this problem. First, the government should make public transport better so that people use it. Second, they can build more roads and flyovers. Also, they can make a rule to reduce cars in the city center.

In conclusion, traffic congestion is a serious problem but it can be solved if the government takes good steps.

Essay 4 (Advantages and disadvantages) · Band 6.0 draft
Prompt: More and more people are working from home. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
Draft: These days, more and more people are working from home. Some people think it has many advantages, but others think it has disadvantages. In my opinion, the advantages are more.

There are many good things about working from home. First, people can save time because they do not need to travel to office. So they can spend this time with family. Second, they feel relaxed and comfortable in their home.

But there are also some bad things. When people work from home, they can feel lonely. Also, sometimes it is difficult to focus because of family and other distractions. Some people also work less.

However, I think the advantages are bigger. With good discipline, people can do their work properly at home. Companies also save money on office rent.

In conclusion, working from home has both good and bad sides, but I believe the advantages are more than the disadvantages.

Essay 5 (Two-part direct question) · Band 6.0 draft
Prompt: Many people today prefer fast food to home-cooked meals. Why is this? Is it a positive or negative development?
Draft: Nowadays, many people prefer fast food instead of home-cooked meals. There are some reasons for this and I think it is a negative development.

There are many reasons why people like fast food. The main reason is that people are very busy today, so they do not have time to cook. Fast food is quick and easy. Another reason is that fast food is tasty and cheap. Also, there are many fast food shops everywhere.

However, I think this is a negative thing. Fast food has a lot of fat and sugar, so it is very bad for health. It causes many diseases like obesity. Home-cooked food is more healthy and clean.

In conclusion, people prefer fast food because it is quick and cheap, but I think it is a negative development because it is bad for our health.

Chapter 6 Part 1 Answer Key
(For the final book, consolidate into Chapter 7. Model answers show one strong version; other accurate, natural rewrites are equally valid.)

Section 1: Sentence Transformations
1. In the modern era, technology plays an indispensable role in our daily lives. (very important thing to indispensable role.)
2. Many people believe that wealth is the key to happiness. (think to believe; money to wealth; tighter phrasing.)
3. Pollution poses a serious threat to public health. (big problem and very bad collapse into a precise collocation.)
4. The government should allocate greater funding to education. (give more money to to allocate greater funding.)
5. A significant proportion of students go abroad in pursuit of well-paid employment. (a lot of to a significant proportion of; a good job to well-paid employment.)
6. Deforestation has a detrimental effect on the environment. (cutting trees to deforestation; very bad thing to detrimental effect.)
7. Children spend excessive time on their phones, which can be detrimental to their development. (vague not good replaced with a precise consequence.)
8. An efficient public transport system can substantially reduce urban traffic congestion. (help to reduce traffic to reduce traffic congestion.)
9. Examinations place considerable pressure on students. (give a lot of pressure to to place considerable pressure on.)
10. Tourism makes a substantial contribution to a nation’s economy. (good for the economy to makes a substantial contribution.)
11. Disadvantaged people often lack access to adequate healthcare. (poor people cannot get good to lack access to adequate.)
12. Social media has fundamentally transformed the way people communicate. (changed the way people talk to transformed the way people communicate.)
13. Although fast food is popular, it gives rise to numerous health problems. (but … causes many to although … gives rise to numerous.)
14. Large corporations should do more to protect the environment. (big companies to large corporations; save to protect.)
15. A command of English is crucial for securing well-paid employment. (learning English is very important for getting a good job to precise nominal phrasing.)
16. The gap between rich and poor continues to widen. (repetitive comparatives replaced with a single precise clause.)
17. Excessive television viewing is an unproductive use of children’s time. (watching too much TV is a waste of time to formal register.)

Section 2: Essay Rewrites (Model Band 8.5 to 9.0)

Essay 1 (Opinion), upgraded:
It is often argued that university education should be provided free of charge to all students. I strongly agree with this view, primarily because it widens access and strengthens the economy in the long run.

The most compelling argument concerns equality of opportunity. At present, many talented young people are unable to attend university because tuition fees are prohibitively expensive. If higher education were free, these students could also pursue their ambitions and secure well-paid employment. Society as a whole would reap the benefits, since a larger pool of skilled graduates drives national productivity.

Admittedly, critics contend that free education places a heavy financial burden on the state, funded ultimately through taxation. They further argue that students may value their studies less when they cost nothing.

Nevertheless, these drawbacks are outweighed by the wider gains. A nation prospers when its population is well educated, and public investment in universities tends to pay for itself through higher earnings and tax revenue. Governments should therefore prioritise funding for higher education.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that university education should be free, as it removes financial barriers for disadvantaged students and yields lasting benefits for the country.

Key upgrades: I am agree to I strongly agree; give importance on to prioritise; but to Admittedly and Nevertheless; a second conditional (if … were free … could); collocations reap the benefits, place a burden on, drive productivity.

Essay 2 (Discuss both views), upgraded:
There is considerable debate about the ideal age for children to begin formal schooling. While some argue that children should start as early as possible, others maintain that a later start is preferable. This essay will examine both views before giving my opinion.

On the one hand, an early start offers clear advantages. Young children absorb new knowledge remarkably quickly, and school helps them develop social skills such as making friends and following rules, which benefit them throughout life.

On the other hand, critics contend that beginning school too soon can be detrimental. Young children need ample time to play and should not face academic pressure prematurely; otherwise, they may lose the freedom of childhood and experience unnecessary stress.

From my perspective, both positions have merit, but the most sensible approach is to strike a balance: children should begin at a moderate age, neither too early nor too late, so that structured learning and free play can coexist.

In conclusion, although opinions on this issue differ, I believe a balanced starting age best serves children’s long-term development.

Key upgrades: discuss about to examine; good points to advantages and merit; bad to detrimental; strike a balance; on the one hand … on the other hand used precisely.

Essay 3 (Problem and solution), upgraded:
Traffic congestion has become a pressing problem in many cities. This essay will outline its principal causes before proposing several viable solutions.

The primary cause is the sheer number of vehicles on the roads. As incomes rise, private car ownership has soared, leaving streets heavily congested. A further factor is inadequate public transport, which pushes commuters toward private cars, while ageing and narrow road networks compound the problem. The consequences are significant: commuters waste countless hours in gridlock, and vehicle emissions worsen urban air quality.

Fortunately, the issue can be addressed. Governments should first invest in efficient mass transit so that commuters have an attractive alternative to driving. Expanding the road network and building flyovers would ease the burden on existing routes. In addition, introducing a congestion charge would discourage private car use in city centres.

In conclusion, although traffic congestion is a serious problem, it can be substantially reduced if authorities implement effective measures, particularly by improving public transport and discouraging unnecessary car journeys.

Key upgrades: very big problem to pressing problem; soared, gridlock, ease the burden, congestion charge, implement effective measures; also to A further factor and In addition.

Essay 4 (Advantages and disadvantages), upgraded:
In recent years, remote working has become increasingly widespread. While it carries certain drawbacks, I firmly believe that its advantages outweigh them.

The benefits are considerable. Firstly, employees no longer need to commute, which saves a great deal of time that can instead be spent with family. Secondly, working in the comfort of one’s own home can reduce stress and improve wellbeing.

Admittedly, there are disadvantages. Remote workers may feel isolated from colleagues, and domestic distractions can make it difficult to concentrate; a minority may also become less productive without direct supervision.

Nevertheless, these drawbacks can largely be overcome. With sufficient self-discipline, most people can work just as effectively from home, and employers benefit too, since they can reduce expenditure on office space. On balance, the flexibility and savings that remote working offers are more significant than its shortcomings.

In conclusion, although working from home has both merits and limitations, I am convinced that its advantages, particularly greater flexibility and reduced commuting, clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

Key upgrades: good things and bad things to benefits and drawbacks; bigger to outweigh; reduce expenditure; On balance; the advantages are more to its advantages clearly outweigh.

Essay 5 (Two-part direct question), upgraded:
These days, a growing number of people favour fast food over home-cooked meals. This essay will explain why this shift has occurred and argue that it is, on balance, a negative development.

Several factors explain the trend. The primary reason is the hectic pace of modern life: many people simply lack the time to prepare meals, and fast food is quick and convenient. In addition, it is inexpensive and palatable, and outlets are now ubiquitous in most cities.

However, I regard this development as largely detrimental. Fast food is typically high in fat, salt, and sugar, and therefore has a harmful effect on health, contributing to conditions such as obesity and heart disease. Home-cooked meals, by contrast, are generally more nutritious and hygienic.

In conclusion, although people increasingly turn to fast food because it is fast and affordable, I believe the trend is a negative one, since it poses a serious threat to public health.

Key upgrades: prefer … instead of to favour … over; tasty to palatable; everywhere to ubiquitous; very bad for health to has a harmful effect on health and poses a serious threat to public health.

Chapter 6: Full Workbook and Self-Assessment (Part 2 of 2)

This second half of the workbook contains five complete Speaking simulations, each with a Part 2 cue card, a model long-turn answer, a set of Part 3 follow-up questions with model answers, and a short lexical analysis. The models are written in natural spoken register, so they use contractions and idioms freely. That is exactly right for Speaking, and exactly wrong for Writing Task 2: notice how the idiomatic language that lifts these answers is the same language Chapter 5 told you to keep out of your essays.

How to use these. Read the cue card, give yourself one minute to plan, then speak for two minutes before reading the model. Record yourself if you can. When you study the model, do not just admire it; underline every idiom and collocation, and check whether you produced anything at that level. The lexical analysis after each model shows you what the examiner would have rewarded.

Simulation 1
Part 2 cue card: Describe a place you enjoy visiting. You should say: where it is; how often you go there; what you do there; and explain why you enjoy visiting it.
Model long-turn answer: I’d like to talk about a small hill town called Bandarban, in the southeast of Bangladesh. It isn’t exactly a stone’s throw away from where I live, so I only manage to go there once in a blue moon, maybe once a year, but it’s always worth the long journey. What I love about it is that it’s completely off the beaten track. While a lot of tourists head to the crowded beaches, Bandarban is quieter and surrounded by breathtaking scenery: green hills, winding rivers, and tiny villages. When I’m there, I usually go hiking, explore the local markets, and just soak up the peace and quiet. The main reason I enjoy it so much is that it gives me a real change of scenery. Living in a busy city, I’m always caught up in the daily grind, so escaping to the hills feels like a breath of fresh air. The last time I went, I reached the top of a hill right at sunrise, and honestly, that view was the icing on the cake. It was almost the trip of a lifetime, and I came back feeling completely recharged.
Part 3 Q1: Why do people enjoy travelling to new places? I think travel broadens people’s horizons. When you visit somewhere unfamiliar, you experience a different culture and way of life, which gives you a fresh perspective. For a lot of people it’s also a chance to escape their routine and recharge, so it’s really the best of both worlds: you relax and you learn something at the same time.
Q2: Does tourism benefit local communities? By and large, yes. Tourism can boost the local economy and create jobs, especially in remote areas. That said, it’s a bit of a double-edged sword, because mass tourism can put a strain on local resources and even degrade natural attractions, so it has to be managed carefully.
Q3: Do people travel more now than in the past? Definitely. Air travel has become far more affordable, and social media makes distant places look appealing, so more people have caught the travel bug. In the past, international travel was a luxury; nowadays, it’s within reach for the average family.
Lexical analysis: The long turn earns its marks through natural idioms (a stone’s throw away, once in a blue moon, off the beaten track, a change of scenery, the daily grind, a breath of fresh air, the icing on the cake, the trip of a lifetime) woven into fluent description, plus the collocation breathtaking scenery. In Part 3 the register shifts slightly toward discussion, bringing in broaden horizons, the best of both worlds, boost the local economy, a double-edged sword, and put a strain on. Every one of these belongs in Speaking; not one belongs in a Task 2 essay.

Simulation 2
Part 2 cue card: Describe a skill you would like to learn. You should say: what the skill is; how you would learn it; how long it might take; and explain why you want to learn it.
Model long-turn answer: A skill I’d really love to learn is playing the guitar. I’ve wanted to pick it up for years, but I’ve never had the time to properly sit down and practise. I’d probably learn it through a mix of online tutorials and a local teacher, because I think I’d need someone to help me get the hang of the basics. I imagine it would be a steep learning curve at first, especially learning the chords, and I’d have to burn the midnight oil to make real progress. Realistically, it might take a year or so before I could play a full song without stumbling. The main reason I want to learn it is that music is a wonderful way to unwind after a long day. At the moment I’m caught up in the daily grind, and I think playing an instrument would help me relax and switch off completely. On top of that, being able to play at family gatherings would be the icing on the cake. Even if I’m never brilliant at it, I’d be over the moon just to strum a few tunes for the people I love.
Part 3 Q1: Is it better to learn a skill from a teacher or by yourself? It depends on the skill, but I think a teacher gives you a real head start. They can spot your mistakes and stop you from picking up bad habits. That said, teaching yourself builds discipline, so ideally you’d combine the two and get the best of both worlds.
Q2: Why do some people find it hard to learn new skills as adults? More often than not, it comes down to time and confidence. Adults are busy and afraid of failing, so they give up before they really get to grips with it. Children, by contrast, learn through trial and error without worrying about looking silly.
Q3: Should schools teach more practical skills? Absolutely. I’d argue that schools place too much emphasis on exams and not enough on practical, transferable skills. Teaching things like budgeting or basic coding would equip students far better for real life.
Lexical analysis: The long turn leans on study and effort idioms (pick it up, get the hang of, a steep learning curve, burn the midnight oil, the daily grind, switch off, the icing on the cake, over the moon) and the natural verb unwind. Part 3 raises the register with a head start, the best of both worlds, get to grips with, trial and error, and the essay-style collocations place emphasis on, transferable skills, and equip students, which show the candidate can move between casual narrative and reasoned argument.

Simulation 3
Part 2 cue card: Describe a piece of technology you find useful. You should say: what it is; how you use it; how often you use it; and explain why it is so useful to you.
Model long-turn answer: The piece of technology I find most useful is, without a doubt, my smartphone. It sounds obvious, but I honestly couldn’t get through the day without it. I use it around the clock, from the moment I wake up to the moment I go to sleep. I rely on it for pretty much everything: checking emails, navigating unfamiliar streets, paying bills, and staying in touch with family. Because so much information is at my fingertips, tasks that used to take hours are now a piece of cake. If I need directions, for instance, I no longer have to ask around; I just tap the screen and go. The main reason it’s so useful is that it’s basically several devices rolled into one, so it saves me a huge amount of time. Of course, it’s a bit of a double-edged sword, because I can easily end up glued to the screen, but as long as I keep it in check, the benefits far outweigh that. For me, it’s genuinely a game changer, and it’s honestly hard to imagine going back to life without it.
Part 3 Q1: Has technology made people’s lives easier or more stressful? It’s genuinely both. On the one hand, technology has transformed the way we work and communicate, making everything faster. On the other, being constantly connected can be exhausting, and a lot of people struggle to switch off. So I’d say it’s a mixed blessing.
Q2: Do you think people rely too much on technology? More often than not, yes. Many of us can’t navigate without a map app or even remember a phone number anymore. It’s convenient, but it does make you wonder whether we’re quietly losing some basic skills along the way.
Q3: How might technology change the way we work in the future? I imagine automation will reshape the job market completely. A lot of routine tasks will be automated, which could render some jobs obsolete, but it should also create brand-new roles. The key will be helping people keep up with the times through proper retraining.
Lexical analysis: The long turn uses tech-flavoured idioms (around the clock, at my fingertips, a piece of cake, a double-edged sword, glued to the screen, keep it in check, a game changer) to sound effortless. Part 3 brings in the formal-leaning collocations transform the way we, a mixed blessing, reshape the job market, render obsolete, and keep up with the times. This is a good illustration of a candidate who can be conversational in Part 2 and more analytical in Part 3 without ever slipping into essay stiffness.

Simulation 4
Part 2 cue card: Describe a time when you helped someone. You should say: who you helped; how you helped them; why they needed help; and explain how you felt about helping them.
Model long-turn answer: I’d like to talk about a time I helped a younger cousin of mine who was struggling with his studies. He was in at the deep end, preparing for a big exam, and he was really down in the dumps because he’d fallen badly behind. I offered to lend a hand and tutor him a couple of evenings a week. We went through the topics he found difficult, and I tried to help him get to grips with the trickier concepts. It wasn’t always a piece of cake, because he’d lost a lot of confidence, so I had to go the extra mile to keep him motivated. He needed help because both his parents worked long hours and couldn’t sit with him, so he’d basically been left to cope on his own. In the end, he pulled his socks up and passed with flying colours. Honestly, I was over the moon when I heard the result. Helping him turned out to be a real labour of love, and seeing him succeed was the icing on the cake. It reminded me just how rewarding it is to give someone a helping hand when they need it.
Part 3 Q1: Why is it important to help others in society? I think helping others creates a stronger sense of community. When people lend a hand, it builds trust and mutual support, which benefits everyone. A society where people only look out for themselves tends to be far more divided.
Q2: Should helping others be taught in schools? Definitely. Schools play a pivotal role in shaping a child’s character, so encouraging students to volunteer instils values like empathy and responsibility. If children learn to help early on, it usually stays with them for life.
Q3: Do people help each other less than they used to? It’s hard to say, but many would argue that busy, urban lifestyles have made people more self-centred. That said, social media has also made it easier to organise help quickly, so in some ways the spirit of helping is alive and well, just in a different form.
Lexical analysis: This long turn is dense with natural idioms because it narrates an experience: in at the deep end, down in the dumps, lend a hand, get to grips with, a piece of cake, go the extra mile, pull his socks up, pass with flying colours, over the moon, a labour of love, the icing on the cake, and a helping hand. Used together but not forced, they signal genuine fluency. Part 3 then reaches for the more academic play a pivotal role in, shaping character, and instil values, which fit an abstract discussion of society.

Simulation 5
Part 2 cue card: Describe an environmental problem in your area. You should say: what the problem is; what causes it; how it affects people; and explain what could be done to solve it.
Model long-turn answer: The biggest environmental problem in my city is air pollution, which has become a really pressing concern over the last few years. On a bad day, the air is so hazy that you can barely see across the street. The main causes are the sheer number of vehicles on the roads and the emissions from nearby factories. Because the city has grown so quickly, the infrastructure simply hasn’t kept up, so traffic is bumper to bumper for most of the day, and all those vehicles emit huge amounts of pollution. It affects people in a big way. Many residents suffer from breathing problems, and children and the elderly are hit the hardest. Honestly, on some mornings it feels like the whole city grinds to a halt under a blanket of smog. As for solutions, I think the authorities need to invest in public transport and gradually discourage private car use, perhaps through a congestion charge. Planting more trees and creating green spaces would help too. It certainly won’t be solved overnight, but if everyone plays their part, I’m hopeful things can improve.
Part 3 Q1: Whose responsibility is it to protect the environment? I’d say it’s a shared responsibility. Governments need to implement effective measures and regulate industry, but individuals also have to play their part by cutting their carbon footprint. Neither side can solve it alone.
Q2: Are people today more environmentally aware than before? By and large, yes. People are far more conscious of issues like climate change, and going green has become quite mainstream. That said, awareness doesn’t always translate into action, so there’s still a long way to go.
Q3: Can technology solve environmental problems? To a certain extent. Renewable energy and cleaner transport are genuine game changers that could mitigate a lot of damage. But technology alone isn’t a silver bullet; it has to go hand in hand with real changes in how we live and consume.
Lexical analysis: Because this topic is closer to an essay theme, the long turn blends natural idioms (bumper to bumper, grinds to a halt, play their part) with topic collocations that also appear in Chapter 4 (a pressing concern, emissions, infrastructure, invest in public transport, discourage private car use, congestion charge, green spaces). Part 3 pushes further into argument language: implement effective measures, carbon footprint, going green, mitigate, a game changer, a silver bullet, and go hand in hand. This shows the useful overlap between Speaking Part 3 and essay vocabulary, while the idioms keep the delivery sounding spoken rather than recited.
